Author: @puurpleeduckk
Content:
TITLE: Why restaurant pasta water is so much better than yours (and how to fix it)

[Opening shot: close-up of spaghetti boiling. Bubbling water sounds.]

ADAM (voice-over):
When people say, “Save your pasta water — it’s liquid gold!” ... they’re not wrong. But I think most home cooks have the wrong idea about why restaurant pasta water is magic.

[Cut to Adam at his counter.]

They think it’s all about the starch. It’s mostly about the starch — but it’s also about salt, and timing, and a little bit of chaos.

SECTION 1: The Myth of the Milky Water

[B-roll: Adam pouring a ladle of cloudy water into a sauce pan.]

In restaurants, that water looks cloudy because they’ve been using it all night. Batch after batch of noodles dumps more starch in there. At home, you cook one pot of pasta, once. So your water’s basically clear — not much starch to emulsify your sauce.

And yeah, you could boil spaghetti for an hour to get that same cloudiness. But then… you’d have mush.

So, the trick isn’t to create more starch; it’s to use what little starch you have more effectively.

SECTION 2: Salt and Boil Dynamics

[Cut to Adam sprinkling salt.]

You’ve probably heard to salt your water “until it tastes like the sea.”
That’s a metaphor. Don’t actually make seawater — that’s way too salty. But you do want it salty enough that you’d drink it and think, “huh, not bad soup.”

Salt affects how the starches gelatinize. Too little salt, and the starch just leaches out without helping your sauce. Too much salt, and the noodles firm up before the starch can even hydrate. Restaurants have dialed this in over thousands of batches.

At home, it’s guesswork — so use about 1.5 tablespoons of kosher salt per gallon, and start from there.

SECTION 3: Controlled Chaos

[B-roll: line cooks tossing pasta.]

Restaurants have another advantage: volume. They’re cooking five things at once. Pasta gets under-boiled a bit, finished in the pan, tossed aggressively. That agitation is key.

When you stir sauce and noodles together, you’re not just mixing — you’re scraping. You’re shaving off microscopic bits of starch and gluten that thicken and bind everything.

That’s why I always tell people: Don’t rinse your pasta. Don’t drain it completely dry. Move it dripping wet into the sauce. Let friction do the emulsifying.

SECTION 4: At-Home Hack

[Cut to Adam at stove.]

So how do you fake restaurant pasta water at home?

Use less water. Seriously — half the volume the box suggests. More concentrated starch.

Finish in the sauce pan. Two minutes before al dente, move it over with tongs and let it simmer in the sauce.

Agitate. Toss, stir, swirl. You can’t over-mix this.

Reserve extra water. Add a splash if the sauce tightens too much.

Do all that, and your sauce will go from watery noodles wearing a coat to noodles living in their sauce.

SECTION 5: Taste Test

[Side-by-side: restaurant vs home pot.]

Let’s taste. Restaurant batch — glossy, clings beautifully. Home batch — a little dull, sauce pools at the bottom.

But the home version after our fixes? Practically identical. The gloss, the cling, the mouthfeel — all there.

SECTION 6: Closing

[Cut back to Adam.]

So yeah, restaurant pasta water is better — because it’s older, saltier, starchier, and gets worked harder.
But with a few small tweaks, your home water can fake it pretty well.

[B-roll of plated spaghetti.]

If you make this, tag me — I love seeing when people actually do the thing instead of just watching the thing.

[Theme music fades in.]

Author: @S0Eric
Content:
I'm often impressed with Adam's fearless communication skills, tackling even controversial topics with fairness and substance. This time, he got a lot right but also included too much opinion and speculation without labeling as such, like he usually does. First, even the experts don't really know how LLMs encode their knowledge. Talking about them as a statistical engines that regurgitate what they consumed may not be completely incorrect, but also not complete enough to be useful. They are trained by running every text source in the world through them, adjusting the internal parameters to predict the next word more accurately. That could imply they are just fancy versions of your phone's "next word" feature. But let's do a thought experiment. Imagine aliens came to earth and left us an individual or computer that was more intellectually capable than us by one or two orders of magnitude. But it didn't know our planet's history or culture, and it hadn't been trained on alien knowledge or general physics. If it read every document we have, wouldn't it understand as much as the most gifted of us combined, and be able to expand on that base of knowledge and understanding? I think everyone would agree that is a reasonable expectation. If a human child can become Stephen Hawking, why wouldn't this more capable alien individual do better? You might argue that reading is different than training to predict the next word, which it is, but you could also argue that if you trained that super intelligent individual by poking it when it predicted the next work incorrectly, and feeding it when it predicted it correctly, it will learn quickly enough. What is the difference between a "next word" statistical engine and actual understanding of everything we know so far? My argument is it's simply one of complexity. When a small language model predicts the next word in an advanced chemistry document, it only has enough capability to choose the next word in a rough statistical manner. But why couldn't a more powerful model reach the highest accuracy by encoding actual understanding of the required topics? Our brains are neural networks. They are amazingly powerful. The difference between a LLM and a human brain is significant, yet similar enough to get to the same place, and beyond eventually, with more complex structures, better simulated neuron behavior, and better training algorithms.

*** More info about LLM training: To perfectly predict the next word in every document, you can simply memorize them. LLMs don't have enough parameters to do that, so they won't predict the correct word exactly every time. But, to achieve high accuracy, they must "understand" the context and concepts.

*** More on hallucinations: If while training that super-capable individual with no moral or cultural foundation, it might start to tell you what it thinks you want to hear. It's also being trained with fictional works. A lot of humans talk nonsense for several reasons, internal and external. Children commonly tell fibs. People of all ages say things that sound good but aren't based on facts. How is this improved? By training and having the individual do further passes over the things it thinks and speaks. This is not an AI specific problem.

Content:
I've been working a lot with LLM's for the past couple of months. They really accelerated my learning in topics i wouldn't have tackled before due to time constraints. I'm using it mainly for working with computers and some physics. Since i have years of experience in those subjects it became clear quite fast that ChatGPT will just make stuff up, when it doesn't understand something. I constantly have to find ways to prevent it from hallucinating stuff. I don't think it ever said "i don't know" when it doesn't actually understand the topic you're asking about. It just presents you something that looks almost exactly like the real explanation that it found in physics textbooks, but all textbooks had minor difference and it doesn't understand those minor difference it ends up making mistakes like switching the definition of variables in the middle of a derivation, which make the entire derivation almost impossible to understand (if you're new to a topic). 
Sometimes it also can't do basic math (addition, subtraction, cosines etc.). You basically have to constantly find ways to check its output for accuracy.

Author: @TheTtmx
Content:
I believe this is a pretty bad job for LLMs. LLMs will not replace you, they won't replace your personality or any of your choices, and I don't think there is a huge point in having them write scripts for you. With this said, I also think that the examples given in the video and in the comments are from people who do not know how to use these tools. Here is my 2 minute attempt.


Title: “The Fastest Gourmet Tuna Melt (That Doesn’t Suck)”

[Opening ambient noise — fridge door opens, mild clatter of plates.]

ADAM (voiceover)
It’s 1:13 PM. I’m hungry. I haven’t showered. And I refuse to pretend that canned tuna is beneath me.

[Cut to tuna can being plonked on the counter.]

This is a tuna melt. Specifically, the fastest, crunchiest, most satisfying version of the tuna melt I’ve managed to reverse-engineer during what is now year four of working from home in pajama pants.

[Cut: Close-up of bread.]

You can use any bread, obviously. But for structure, I’m going with this dense sourdough slab from the bakery that I pretend is for special occasions but actually just means it was on sale.

Slice. Toast the inside surfaces first. This keeps the sandwich from turning into a tuna sponge. Butter goes in the pan, medium heat.

[Cut: Butter melting, bread face-down.]

If you’re wondering why I’m pre-toasting before I even add the tuna — welcome. This is your first Ragusea video, isn’t it?

[Cut: Bowl and can of tuna.]

Standard water-packed tuna. Drain it. Don’t rinse it. I know people do that — don’t. That water has flavor. You're throwing away flavor.

And now: one tablespoon of mayo. A squeeze of Dijon. Black pepper. Maybe a squirt of lemon or pickle brine if you're feeling frisky. No celery. This is not a salad bar.

[Cut: Tuna mixture being stirred.]

Mash it just until it binds. If it looks too creamy, you’ve gone too far. You want it like... wet stuffing.

[Cut: Bread is out, assembly starts.]

Okay. Inside face gets a thin shmear of mustard or hot sauce, or whatever makes your mouth feel feelings. Tuna goes on.

Now: cheese.

Sharp cheddar. Gruyère if you’re the kind of person who owns an olive oil pourer. I like a blend. Put the cheese under and over the tuna. This isn't structural. It’s psychological.

[Cut: Sandwich goes into pan, now with top slice.]

Back in the pan, low and slow. Lid on. You want it to melt inside before the outside burns. This takes like... five minutes. Use that time to question your life choices. Or, if you’re me, promote the sponsor.

[Sponsor Segment — fictionalized in style]
Speaking of efficient choices, this video is sponsored by "BreadBuddy" — no joke, it’s a thing that keeps your sandwich bread fresh without turning it into cardboard. Because while I do love dense sourdough, 90% of you are using plastic-bagged supermarket loaves. No judgment. BreadBuddy. Link below. Thank you, BreadBuddy.

[Cut: Sandwich flip.]

Flip. Admire. That’s the color. If it’s not deeply golden, you’re rushing the process.

And now the magic touch. Take your spatula, press down gently. You’re not smashing a burger. Just a little squish, just enough to make it feel intentional.

Pull it off. Let it rest. Trust me.

[Cut: Cross section.]

Slice. Show off the cheese pull. The tuna’s warm, the cheese is molten, the bread is crisp.

[Adam taste-testing.]

Yep. Still the best lunch I can make in under 15 minutes with canned fish.

[Closing with Lauren walking in.]

LAUREN (off-camera)
That smells so good. Did you actually toast the bread first this time?

ADAM
Yes. Yes, I did.

[Cut to end screen.]


I do think there are some weird sentences, but in general it feels Raguseasy~

Author: @thomasgebert6119
Content:
Amazing! Adam has a consistent and strict definition of what "reasoning" and what "knowing something" means enough to assert that AI doesn't.  He should alert the neuroscience community and collect his inevitable Nobel Prize. 

I also love how you keep asserting that training data is "piracy".  Weird how you didn't claim that Google Books and Google Scholar are piracy, despite them also scanning and indexing copyrighted works without permission.  Oh, is it because this has actually been tried in court and it was determined to be transformative? Maybe?  These kind of arguments are going to be what Disney uses to eventually outlaw fair use and using "inspiration" as a defense, like they have been trying to do my entire life. 

This is a big pet peeve of mine for the anti-AI people.  They just assert shit, and make shit up as axioms, and then act like it's obvious when it very much isn't obvious to *anyone* who has *actually* learned anything about this technology instead of watching three videos on youtube and pretending they're an expert. 

"Statistical Text Generation" more accurately describes a Markov Chain, which has never been state of the art with regards to text generation, which is why it was largely relegated to stuff like iOS autocomplete for most of computer science history.  In 2016 people pejoratively compared Donald Trump's tweeting style and speaking patterns to a Markov chain because it *did* feel like a statistical auto-complete.

In an *extremely* hand wavey way this sort of describes LLMs + transformers, but it's like claiming that baking and blacksmithing are basically the same thing because they both involve working with a material and putting it in an oven. They're different things that have some superficial similarities. 

ChatGPT and DeepSeek do something that, at least superficially, appears to resemble reasoning.  I know about as much about neuroscience as you do, Adam, so I'm not going to actively claim that it is and isn't reasoning. 

Honestly, the number of unsubstantiated claims in here sort of makes this video feel like it was written by AI.

Author: @kademadeintheshade8456
Content:
Something that bothers me in GenAI discussions is the overall lack of nuanced views on the subject. While I’m personally cautiously optimistic about GenAI, I feel like everyone speaking on the issue is either vehemently opposed to AI or naively defensive of it, so this video was really refreshing. 

I don’t think GenAI is inherently bad, but we have to be cautious and stay cognizant of how it actually works and what it’s suitable for. It’s excellent at summarization, data analysis, repetitive tasks(coupled with RPA, e.g.), and it’s very adaptable. While this has the potential to grow the economy in ways that benefit all of us, it also has the potential to drive automation and job displacement that industrial growth can’t keep up with. This is why I say I’m cautiously optimistic rather than “totally pro-AI” as some of the tech bros do. On the flip side, a lot of anti-AI absolutism seems to echo arguments for technological regression and degrowth, which I think are also dangerous concepts.

Overall, I don’t think it’s productive to be scared of AI. Like every other technology, its potential to both hurt or help society is dependent on  how we humans apply it. 

Thanks for the cool video Adam!

Author: @Vote4Drizzt
Content:
Because of the way LLMs currently work, part of the "magic" that lets them do what they do is basically trading deterministic methods of getting answers, what you and I would consider learning or knowledge processes, with a kind of blind inference from all of it's data. 

This results in a system that can answer questions that have complex and nuanced answers with surprising accuracy because there are connections we don't fully understand between the sum of many questions and the answer to any individual one. But because randomness has to be part of the process, it also produces systems that, some percentage of the time, get established facts completely wrong. I recall one conversation in which a person claimed some early models could answer interesting questions in some depth but if asked repeatedly asked if 4 was prime, claimed that it was 1% of the time(or whatever percentage).

It's as if we've traded an ability to guess at more complex answers using statistical tricks for the ability to answer simple factual questions without error. I think if we quit sourcing the data unethically and look where places where a surprisingly good guess is valuable, there will be use cases. As it stands, Claude from Anthropic can talk to me about 3d printing and FPV drones in surprising depth. It just also suggests things that completely fail the sniff test. Copilot generates short scripts or code snippets for me but I can only safely let it save me time(forgetting syntax, dealing with formatting etc), because  I already know how to do the work and I can spot check for trash answers. Anytime the tool is doing something I cannot already do very well, suddenly I have to take it at face value. So the use is obviously *not* what people want it to be, but that doesn't mean there is no use in principal.

Again, until we can figure out how to source data for it without screwing anyone, no in-principal use case is worth it. I just have spent a lot of time trying to find the tool inside the cloud of bullshit around it. I think there *is* something to this technology but it's not going to replace us all. Finding what it *can* do and mastering it might be good for my career though.

Author: @ThatCrookedMind
Content:
Though I really appreciate your criticism of AI from a more journalistic point of view, I think it may fail to reach the true core of the problem. I believe that though the issues you bring up are huge problems today, it's inevitable that they will be ironed out AT SOME POINT. Granted, a lot of damage will be done on the way, but I think eventually these models will be really good at fact checking and ultimately stop hallucinating. 
I believe that the biggest issue with AI is that it is slowly removing process from the human equation. I work in the creative industry and gen AI is already destroying whole industries at an alarming rate. Things tend to flow down the path of less money spent and more money made and brands have no problem substituting human work for AI if the results are good, and the results are getting pretty damn good. 
As you know from cooking, a huge part of the value in it comes from the process. You make mistakes, you learn, you invest time, energy and money into it, and in the end you don't just get a meal, you get a lot more. 

I think it was Yuval Noah Harari that said that what makes him scared of AI is not that it will rise up and kill us Terminator style, but that it's slowly killing our humanity.

Author: @Monoffel
Content:
Hello, self-proclaimed Adam Ragusea fan here (not the one who sent that email). I'm also a fan of AI. I also work with AI sometimes (more than just prompting it). We all know there is no shortage of AI bs out there, and I can't even claim that AI is a net benefit to humanity. But I have to point out here that they are not "glorified auto complete". This is a common argument, that does not hold any real substance.

You bolster this view, by stating that you are pretty sure that LLMs statistically generate the next token, and that you are pretty sure that this what makes the core of an LLM. (I'm just paraphrasing). You then add some conclusions, like that LLMs cannot reason, and they cannot lie (the implication being that they don't even qualify for the level of awareness necessary to be able to lie).

While technically true on some level, that they statistically generate tokens, this mechanism cannot be used to explain that they are worse than human brains in their abilities. It is neither the case that we can prove that humans don't do this (except on some technical level that doesn't change the conclusions), nor that this mechanism is inferior to human intelligence or consciousness.

For example, ask a very difficult yes/no question. How does a human answer this? They may do a large number of intermediate computations (analagous to outputting tokens) in their head, before staying either "yes" or "no". But ultimately, that answer is also statistical. They did the math, and they responded with the most likely answer. So in other words, that binary choice is a statistical answer. As an LLM opponent, you may now try to go retreat to the domain of math, where in some sense statistics is eliminated from the answers. But even there, we neither know if we really exist, on a philosophical level, and we always work with axioms in math as well, which is to say that statistics cannot be meaningfully escaped from. The human brain hallucinates reality, to the extent that we can never be sure if our existence came to be just a moment ago, with all your memories synthetically inserted. What we really are is brains in a dark, lightless jar, with some sensory inputs piped into it, and some motor outputs coming out of it.

Anyway, if you really want to cling to math, then this argument gets challenging, but certainly in most fields, humans can be brought into situations where they statistically output an answer. Any kind of multiple choice scenario, for example. You could argue that outside such scenarios, we do not statistically generate tokens/thoughts. But what I'm saying is it doesn't matter what you call it, our thoughts can be conceptually represented as tokens. Even in "large X models", tokens can be text, images, sound, and even bytes. Tokens are not inherently text, and so we can conceptually also label what our brain does in its thought process as tokens. You may want to cling to the sequentiality of tokens, as a defense for the uniqueness of the human brain, saying "But our thoughts are not one token after the other, it's a lot more complex than that". But you can make an LLM do the same thing. For example, prompt your question to an LLM multiple times at once, and then aggregate those outputs back into a single one at the end. Now you have some sort of parallelism, like you might have in a human brain.

If you're interested in the differences and similarities of biological and artificial neural networks, Geoffrey Hinton is a very smart person who dedicates his life to this topic. You can find arguments from him about the learning process, i.e. back-propagation, and whether our brains conceptually do this, for example. (Though his conclusion is utlimately that it doesn't really matter, because backprop is equal or better to the human learning process in its capabilities.)

To summarise, just because the process is statistical in nature, it does not follow that it's "dumb" or "not conscious", or inferior to human thinking. I'm not disagreeing that the best current LLMs are dumb and I wouldn't call them all that conscious either, but you can't categorically say that they can't ever be intelligent due to the statistical nature.

Moreover, even *today* , you can do so much more with an LLM, than what this fan mailed to you with excitement. This may not be obvious to you, if you've never programmatically used LLMs before. But for example, take a modern reasoning model. Whether the name reasoning is qualifies for reasoning doesn't matter. But what matters is that they have a mechanism to *revise* mistakes. A scratchpad of ideas, that they can use, before coming up with an answer. To a fault, this scratchpad is still sequential in nature, but it's simple enough to remove this limitation. And even with it being sequential, I think a lot of people would be surprised what you can do with this. The reasoning block will have "thoughts" like "but wait ...", "alternatively...", where the model is able to explore different directions, *before coming up with an answer.* I can't emphasize enough how similar this is to human thinking, and how apparent it distances LLMs from the whole "glorified auto complete" paradigm. If the model can step through various ideas, rather than just saying a single "yes/no" answer, then what is the point of labeling it "statistical" (with the meaning statistical = dumb)? This is exactly what a human would do. Sure, a human could rapid-fire a gut yes/no response, but most of the time, they would do the same exact process, of exploring different angles, and reasoning through them, before giving an answer.

Even if a human would to a gut response, what would this response be based on, if not the statistical life experience of that human? Much like the LLM response would be the statistical response of what it learned.

If you wanted to create a better dam Ragusea video script with AI, here are some pointers:
* instruct the AI to have a childlike or not-so-serious persona - this makes it more likely to admit mistakes, rather than doubling down
* use a reasoning model for idea generation, and use a writing model to imitate Adam's style writing
* supply examples of Adam's writing, at least initially, if not periodically - it may have ingested YT video subtitles in its training, but even then the "statistical" process often merges it into some sort of average
* generate *more* tokens - a so called 0-shot prompt, where you ask a single question, and take that output as final, will always give you something that is short in length - the most obvious workaround to that is to just ask it to generate a part, then another part, and so on
* ask it to create a rough draft of the script first, with its chapters, then have it refine that script over multiple prompts
* then for each chapter, ask it to generate the content as a draft first, then refine it
* since we want to be "fair" to the process, in the sense that the AI has to do most of the work by itself, and we want to just sit back and watch, make heavy use of self-reflection - ask the model to revise its prior outputs until sufficient

All of the above can be mostly accomplished in a linear fashion, but if you wanted to go real serious, you would program an agent framework:
* you assign multiple "agents", which you can think of as instances of the same LLM, but each with its own goal and conversation history
* one agent ideates, one writes, one revises or proceeds, and several simply validate with different criteria (e.g. match the Adam style, match the humor, match the desired length, verify narrative consistency, etc.)
* these agents are then arranged in a loop to work together collaboratively
* if you assign the roles and define the goals and criteria sufficiently, in theory this agent framework can now spend e.g. all night to come up with a script, without any human invervention

(Note that the complexity of agentic frameworks greatly exceeds that of basic prompting techniques, and would require one or multiple people who really know what they're doing. It's not really practical today, but all big companies are researching in this area)

Now if you wanted to take it further still, you would "post-train" a model on Adam's writing samples directly. This is even more technically challenging, since now you have to deal with training models, where a lot can go wrong, it's expensive, and you are also locking yourself down to a particular model. Up until now, you could always plug in the latest models. But if you ever successfully train a model, it will now be very specific in producing output in the Adam Ragusea style. (It will also likely have forgotten almost everything else). This now unburdens you from having to provide writing samples, which in turn gives you extra room in your context. Context is analogous to short-term memory, and it is also a limited quantity, that has to be considered at all times, in each conversation history. Another practical workaround here is to offer the model a permanent storage as long-term memory. But this would likely be overkill for this project.

If you've done all this, and the scripts you get still suck, well then you still can't say that LLMs are fundamentally incapable, but at least you would have explored what current models are capable of, to the full extent. All of which is to constrast this with the 2023 video script you've got, and how much more AI can do.

Author: @bosstowndynamics5488
Content:
I think one thing that frequently gets missed in these conversations about LLMs and generative AI is the corporate/financial side of the issue, and that's a real shame because IMHO it's by far *the* most important part. The reason it's getting pushed this hard is because these big tech companies want to sell you these things as a service they can charge subscriptions for, which results in rampant abuse and overuse for things it really shouldn't be used for, made worse by the fact that all these services are operating at a loss as they're concerned solely with gaining market share and are working off the assumption they'll be able to turn a profit in the future, so the price for spammers and content mils to use them to generate massive amounts of "content" without any real effort, fact checking or creative intent involved is far lower than the real cost of using them, which makes it much easier to flood the internet with it. If you look at what's happening in the open source space though with free tools developed off of these models and what keen hobbyists are doing with them for information processing and yes, even creative uses (creative uses that include original effort and intent, mind, that's the key difference between this and just pumping out a ton of images generated from basic prompts), *that's* where the actual interesting uses are, and I'm firmly of the belief that the biggest difference here is that there's no profit motive - these are tools being made and shared *for free* by hobbyists who are genuinely interested in using these tools to get stuff done rather than mass marketing it to make money. And because there's no profit incentive they're generally not just trying to directly copy artists' work, they're at least trying to do unique things with it in a way that's far more defensible as fair use, and they're by and large not incentivised to try and steal the market of the original artists to grab market share.

Tl;dr the problem isn't really the LLMs/image generators/AI, the problem is who is using them and the framework in which they're operating.

Author: @jamggurogi42
Content:
I used to be proud when I had to explain that the topic of my PhD was AI. Now I have to give a disclaimer that AI is actually a very interesting and diverse scientific field, and I don't work on solution-in-search-of-a-problem chat bots that are now popularly considered to be the meaning of "AI". It's sad to see our cool field get hijacked like this... it makes me, a scientist in AI, hate every product that mentions AI! Maybe this is what nuclear physicists went through when their scientific field became synonymous with bombs and apocalypses as the meaning of "nuclear", but at least nuclear weapons are actually effective at their advertised goal (it's just not a very nice one).

For those who care, AI is not a new field, it's a very diverse field spanning many disciplines that has been around for decades. Nearly every single thing you own depends on AI at some point in its development. These are very good things with clear use cases, and I fully encourage embracing the technology there!

But when it comes to the LLM chat bots, they're overhyped, anthropomorphised, and pushed very strongly by companies. Like "smart appliances", in most cases I doubt they add these components because they will result in a better consumer experience. It's just another way of harvesting more data, and engineering dependence on the companies so that basic things you could already do become a subscription service that can be monetised. 

Such a sad fate of the scientific field to be reduced to such a cynical image in the public eye... which we have companies, not consumers, to thank for.

Author: @jomo9454
Content: This is a good take on AI but I think the technical details of how they work is a bit different from statistical next word prediction. Each bit of information that we would think of as a word has all these connections drawn to other words related to it, but they're called tokens. The token we would call nose has a link to body parts, a link to breathing, a link to smell, a link to the face, a link to the English spelling "nose", a link to animals, a link to the concept of vocal quality changes described as "nasal" in English, a link to a token representing the Spanish word nariz, and the arrows pointing to all the related concepts have numbers attached representing how strongly they're linked. Of course the less the training the fewer the links to related tokens and the less representative of general text the associations will be. That's why it mostly makes some kind of sense, while next likely word quickly yields incoherence. This is also why it doesn't even know truth from fiction - almost zero concepts have any steadfast relationship with being "true" or "false"... I mean... is the concept of a turtle true or false? It doesn't even make sense to ask. Likewise the concept of the possibility Oswald had help isn't true or false. The concept of Detective Sherlock Holmes isn't itself true or false, but a token for Sherlock Holmes the character would have an arrow pointed at the concept of fictional characters, so the llm would know Sherlock Holmes stories are fiction. And so it would assess the story of "Sherlock Holmes Being Written" as a fictional Sherlock Holmes story UNLESS there was a token for that story with arrows pointed at tokens for non-fiction, literature about the author Arthur Conan Doyle, etc. That's why when they don't have enough training or if they have too much they screw up - not enough and the nearest tokens they find aren't closely related enough, too much training in the wrong areas (imagine thousands of old phone books) and too many tokens will have the same first, middle, and last name tokens associated and it can't track which person token it's talking about.

Author: @dylangrullon234
Content:
As someone still on the fence of the moral value of these new AI bots, I feel inclined to point out 2 areas AIs are at least starting to move past the constraints you mentioned:
* reasoning/agent models: basically repeated prompts fed back to itself. rather than trying to 1 shot an answer, it approximates a thought process to break down problems and verify intermediate results. particularly impressive for coding - where the ai can recognize errors and self correct them. watching these is pretty spooky because of how closely it mirrors the actual process humans use, not just spitting out something that approximates their final result
* deep research: new modes that perform a significant number of web searches to find, summarize, and importantly cite its results. takes a potentially long time to run, but is surprisingly good at generating useable and well cited background research

Now whether these can fully overcome the constraints and even the moral flaws you mention is clearly still up for debate, but in fairness they are at least trying. It seems unfortunately inevitable these tools are here to stay...

Author: @grp215
Content:
I very much dislike the implication that LLMs are "auto complete." I feel like it underminds the capabilities of AI, which is actually counter to stances against it. You can ask an LLM things like "a baby walks a few steps before falling down. It's smiling and laughing. Why would the baby respond this way?" It will tell you it's proud of its first steps. You can say "a man finds himself in a long hallway. There are many doors. Very bright lights shine from the ceiling every ten feet." You ask what the man does next, and you can DM an entire roll play session where the AI explores this environment. If you say something weird like "you have to eat the bird to escape this room" it won't and will proceed to act "nervously" as if its worried it will have to do something against its protocols. Make of that what you will, but calling this "auto complete" or "predicting the next most likely word" is too close to misdirection for my comfort.

To clarify, I don't think Adam or most people are intentionally misdirecting anyone. It's just a popular oversimplification that leads to misconceptions.

Author: @Shadowmech88
Content:
I've recognized this issue from day 1, and it's why it confuses me so much when laypeople use LLMs for asking questions. They treat it like a search engine like Google. Do they just not know?

Like you say, anyone can make an error. But when I google a question, maybe my answer is in a Reddit post which can have other people attesting its correctness. Maybe my answer is in an article written by someone who has real credentials that make it more likely that they are the sort of person to be properly informed or more diligent about fact-checking everything. Maybe my answer is in a Wikipedia page that not only has citations to outside sources, but has had multiple sets of eyes on it ensuring that everything is reasonably correct.
An LLM's answer has none of these assurances. I simply have to trust that its statistically-driven text prediction happened, by chance, to get the factually correct answer. Which it does a lot of the time, but not _every_ time, and that means that I always have to second-guess and verify the LLM's answer myself. And if I'm having to do a web search to verify the LLM's answer myself, then what was the point of asking it in the first place?

The issue of accuracy seems like a pretty fatal flaw for 90% of the uses that people purport for LLMs, and I don't think it's something that can be fixed with more data either. It seems like a core issue with the technology, with the fact that LLMs are just complex predictive text generators. LLMs can be great for churning out creative writing, I'm sure, but the idea of using LLMs for applications that need to be based in _reality_ seems like a dead end.

Author: @Siinocei
Content:
Hey Adam, love your videos long-time watcher, first-time commenter.

This comment will probably be out of date in six months. The field of AI is moving at breakneck speed.

That said, I want to point out a few issues with how people tend to talk about AI. AI isn’t a reporter, an author, or even a fiction writer. It's Jakob the really smart intern who’s read a ton across a wide range of topics. He’s built up internal models of how the world works and tends to answer with a lot of confidence. But Jakob isn’t alone. There’s also Mark, Twain, and Fernando each better at different things. Twain, for instance, has a huge memory. You can hand him an entire book or study, and he’ll pull useful information from it with minimal hallucination.


This is the key issue: yes, you can use AI as a fabulism generator, but if you learn how to wield it, it becomes an excellent research assistant. Twain might know quite a bit about a topic, but if you catch him at the pub and ask for his sources, he’ll rattle off a list some accurate, some misremembered, and a few that might not even exist, especially if it’s something he looked up weeks ago.

One of the fundamental misunderstandings in this video even in the example about the Ragusea script is the expectation that AI should just remember what Adam did. The fact that later versions can even half-replicate your style is remarkable. Try asking the average person on the street to do the same after watching two of your videos a while back. Their take will be generic “YouTuber” voice at best. You’ll get a much stronger result by giving the model a script.

AIs aren’t just next-word prediction engines. They operate in a conceptual vector space where semantically related words cluster together, and where the distance between two ideas (like “man” to “woman” and “king” to “queen”) reflects broader structural relationships. They thus have an implicit understanding of concepts.

AI can’t be shamed, but during training, one thing companies often select for is truthfulness which, by the way, can be a semi-antagonistic variable when balanced against politeness or pro-social phrasing.

And today’s LLMs aren’t even just LLMs anymore they’re multimodal models. They consume not just text but also images and video. They now have tooling too. Imagine being stuck in a black box with no memory of the world but someone lets you glance at a phone to check the time and date. That’s what tool use looks like for an AI. And this is just the beginning developers are adding things like physics simulations into the mix now with newer models heading towards becoming world models.

Anyway, just some thoughts on how we frame the conversation around these tools.

The first implies a qualitative similarity, and could be more precisely written "salty like the sea", we aren't making a brine, but it should be salty enough to not taste good for drinking. The second implies a more quantitative similarity, you could measure both to see which is saltier, or if they are as salty as each other. The phrase should help people to remember to salt the water for boiling pasta, and to salt it more heavily than most food should be salted because of how much of the salt doesn't make it into the pasta.

I don't think AI can understand that kind of distinction, and maybe never will.

Author: @danielriley7193
Content:
An interesting tangent: Our modern popular understanding of "a Luddite" as someone with a broad and baseless rejection of technological advancement is actually a propagandistic lie. The historical Luddites were a fascinating labor movement in the textiles industry in 19th-century England who were protesting, not against technology broadly, but against specific machines that were mechanizing the textile industry and that, notably, produced markedly inferior products to what had until then been the norm, but could do so quickly and cheaply, thus threatening a labor force that had consisted of skilled and well-paid artisans with mass unemployment during a period of instability and high costs of living caused by the Napoleonic Wars, and for at best debatable benefit to anyone but the capitalists who owned the machines. Interesting characters and details abound, including but not limited to: the movement's fictional figurehead, the apocryphal "Ned Ludd" that gives them their name; the Luddites resorted to breaking into factories at night to destroy machines after public protesters were shot in the streets, one of the earliest examples of industrial sabotage; in response, Parliament made "machine-breaking" a capital crime in 1812;  the involvement of famous literary persona Lord Byron, who vociferously defended the Luddites in the House of Lords and criticized the government's response.

Essentially, Adam's stance of well-founded skepticism regarding this particular technology is actually very much in line with the historical Luddites, and we should reject the simplistic narrative that paints the Luddite label as a pejorative. As the kids might say, the Luddites were based, actually.

Spaghetti Carbonara: The 15-Minute Roman Classic That Everyone Screws Up

A Tuesday night in the kitchen. Let's make carbonara — the Roman pasta dish that's basically scrambled eggs with cheese, except when you do it right, it's silk. This is one of those recipes where technique matters more than ingredients, which is great because you probably have everything already.
Here's what we need: spaghetti, eggs, pecorino romano cheese, guanciale or pancetta, and black pepper. That's it. No cream, no peas, no chicken — just those five things. Any Italian grandmother would hunt you down if you added cream to this.
Start with about a quarter pound of guanciale. This is cured pork jowl, and it's what makes carbonara taste like carbonara instead of cheesy scrambled eggs. Can't find guanciale? Pancetta works. Bacon? Fine, but you're making bacon pasta, not carbonara — the smokiness changes everything. Cut it into matchsticks — we want pieces that'll render their fat slowly and get properly crispy.
Cold pan, cold fat — that's my approach for even rendering. Some cooks start with a hot pan, but I like the control you get with gradual heat. Medium-low is critical here — high heat will toughen that beautiful pork into little rubber nuggets. You'll hear it start to sizzle and pop. That's pig fat turning into liquid gold. Don't rush this — good carbonara takes patience, bad carbonara happens when you're in a hurry.
Here's where I break from tradition slightly: toss in a crushed garlic clove or two with the guanciale. Purists will scream, but that gentle garlic flavor in the rendered fat adds another layer. Fish it out before you add the pasta — we want the essence, not the chunks.
While that's going, get your pasta water boiling. Here's where everyone gets weird about salt — you don't need to make it taste like the Atlantic Ocean. Just salt it like you would any pasta water. Enough so it tastes seasoned when you sip it, not like you're drinking seawater.
Now the magic part — the egg mixture. Here's where Romans get religious about technique. For maximum silkiness, we're going all-yolk — about 5 to 6 egg yolks for a pound of pasta. The whites actually work against us here, making the sauce less creamy. Save those whites for tomorrow's scrambled eggs.
Grate your pecorino fine — and I mean fine. Big chunks won't melt properly and you'll end up with lumpy sauce. About three-quarters cup of pecorino, but here's my secret: mix in a quarter cup of good parmesan. Pure pecorino can be aggressively salty, and the parm mellows it out. If you want a slightly lighter sauce color — and only if you want — add a teaspoon of milk to the mixture. Purists will roll their eyes, but sometimes presentation matters.
Whisk it all together until it looks like thick yellow paint. Now comes the pepper — and I mean a lot of pepper. We're talking nearly a tablespoon of coarsely ground black pepper, not fine dust. This isn't just seasoning, it's one of the defining flavors of carbonara. You should see black specks throughout that golden mixture.
Your guanciale should be golden and crispy now. Turn off the heat — this is crucial. Hot pan will scramble your eggs faster than you can say "carbonara disaster."
Drop your spaghetti in the water. While it cooks, here's the technique that separates great carbonara from cafeteria pasta: tempering. Take a ladle of hot pasta water and slowly whisk it into your egg mixture. This warms up the eggs gradually so they won't scramble when they hit the pasta. Add another ladle, keep whisking. The mixture should be loose and creamy now.
Pasta's done when it's just shy of al dente — it'll finish cooking in the pan. Here's the crucial part: reserve at least a full cup of that starchy pasta water before you drain anything. This isn't just water anymore — it's liquid gold with dissolved starches that'll bind your sauce. Don't you dare pour it all down the drain like some amateur.
Here's where most people panic, and honestly, I get it. Remove your pan from heat entirely and let it cool for about 30 seconds. Hot pan plus raw eggs equals scrambled disaster. Pasta goes into the pan with the rendered guanciale and that beautiful garlic-infused fat. Toss it around, let every strand get coated.
Now pour in your egg mixture and start tossing like you're conducting an orchestra. The residual heat from the pasta will cook the eggs just enough to create that silky sauce. If it's looking too thick, add that reserved pasta water bit by bit — the starch will help everything come together. Too thin? Keep tossing, maybe put it back on the lowest heat for just a few seconds, stirring constantly.
The sauce should coat every strand of spaghetti but still flow like silk, not cling like glue. If you need to reheat slightly, do it gently with constant motion — we're tempering eggs, not making breakfast. Taste it — you might need more cheese, more pepper, maybe a tiny pinch of salt though the guanciale and cheese probably have you covered.
Plate it immediately — carbonara is the diva of pasta dishes, it absolutely refuses to wait. Hit it with a final generous crack of black pepper on top, maybe a little extra cheese if you're feeling generous. If you grabbed some fresh sage or rosemary while that guanciale was rendering, now's the time to tear a few leaves over the top. Just a whisper of fresh herbs to brighten the richness.
This is what Rome tastes like at midnight when you're too tired to cook but too hungry to care. It's comfort food that happens to be elegant, peasant food that tastes like luxury. The kind of dish that makes you understand why Italians get so particular about their recipes — because when something's this simple, every detail matters.
And that's carbonara. No cream, no confusion, just eggs and cheese and pork fat turned into something that'll make you question every pasta dish you've ever ordered at a chain restaurant. The technique is everything here — master the temperature control, respect the starchy pasta water, and you've got a dish that's both ancient and impossibly sophisticated.

Author: @nir_aviv
Content:
Apart from the super understandable concerns about training data rights, I don't quite understand this discussion... I think that you know to a good degree what these tools are, their limitations and what they're good for. Why hold them to journalistic standards? Why expect to generate final, trustable results instead of very fast, sometimes good and sometimes imperfect drafts? It would be great if they could do more, but it's certainly not necessary...

And even with the flood of "AI slop", I don't feel that the situation is much worse today than it used to be. You'll always need sources that you trust to sign off on the information you consume, unless you verify it yourself... this is as true today as it was 10 years ago. You didn't believe the 99% of random crap from untrusted sources that filled the internet then, and you still don't. If that's not true for someone, then that sounds to me like a literacy problem.

On the other hand - now you have, yes, just a powerful autocomplete, but that's valuable because it can let people work a lot faster. In my experience I view it as a gas pedal - it can absolutely steer me in the wrong direction, but that's ok - I correct it when needed. And in return I can get a reasonable starting point, in seconds, for small enough tasks. I use it to brainstorm, and I vet everything, iterate and clarify as needed, and in the end I've completed work in days that would have taken me weeks otherwise. That's a big economic and personal boost that shouldn't be discounted.

[Opening shot: Adam in his kitchen, casual tone]

They thought I wouldn’t find it. Embedded under the skin. Standard issue data implant. I’ve seen these before. Langley, 2011.

[Cut to close-up of wine bottle — barcode scans itself]

I’m out of time.

Author: @scottmckeown1729
Content:
I know a lot of people are upset about AI—especially artists, whether they work with words or visuals or sound. And I get it. It's hard watching the path to making a living through creativity become narrower by the day. If that trend continues, it may feel like there’s no room left to create art for income at all.

But for what it's worth, I'm a janitor. And I'm fairly confident that within 20 years (give or take), robots powered by AI will be able to do my job better and cheaper than I can. At that point, I probably won’t have a job.

If that happens, I don’t expect most people will rally behind me with “But janitors have a right to make a living!” Some might. But I think most would view it as just another phase of progress—one that raises productivity and (hopefully) the standard of living overall.

That said, I don’t support massive economic shifts that happen too fast. Rapid change always hurts the people who are least able to absorb the shock. But in principle, if we support AI replacing blue-collar jobs to improve society, isn’t it worth asking why we draw the line at creative ones?

If we ever do reach a point where almost everyone is making art as their primary economic output… well, that doesn’t sound sustainable or fair. We'd need something like universal basic income just to keep society stable. And in that world, nearly all art would be made not for profit, but for passion, curiosity, or to stave off boredom.

And honestly? The passion art and the interest art... that’s the art I want to see. I don't watch Adam Ragusea because it pays his bills. It is entertaining because his topics interest him and often he feels passion about the topics.

## The Potato Salad That's Better For You Tomorrow: The Science of Resistant Starch

**(Video opens with a close-up shot of Adam at his kitchen counter. He's holding a single, humble-looking boiled potato.)**

**Adam Ragusea:** This potato. It’s a pretty simple food, right? Boiled, maybe a little salt. You’ve probably eaten a hundred of them in your life. But what if I told you that by doing one simple, almost counterintuitive thing to this potato, you could fundamentally change how your body uses it? And in the process, make it a whole lot friendlier to your gut?

**(He places the potato down.)**

Now, if you've been watching my channel for a while, you might remember a video I made a few years back about something called "resistant starch." The whole "carb with no calories... kinda" thing. And in that video, I talked about the science of how certain starches can resist digestion and become food for the good bacteria in your gut.

But since then, the science has gotten even more interesting, and I've been experimenting with ways to really maximize this effect in my own kitchen. Because, let's be honest, telling you to eat a raw potato or a green banana is... well, it's not very practical, is it?

**(He gestures to the camera with a self-deprecating smile.)**

So today, I'm going to show you a very delicious, very practical way to get more of this good stuff into your diet. We're going to make a potato salad. But this isn't just any potato salad. This is a potato salad that is scientifically better for you if you eat it tomorrow.

**(Title card: The Potato Salad That's Better For You Tomorrow)**

**(Scene change: Adam is now at his stove with a pot of boiling water.)**

So, the first step is pretty straightforward. We're going to boil some potatoes. I'm using some waxy potatoes here, your Red Bliss, your new potatoes. They hold their shape a little better, which is what you want in a potato salad. But honestly, use whatever potatoes you have. The "good enough" philosophy applies, as always.

**(He adds the potatoes to the pot.)**

Now, while these are cooking, let's talk a little more about what's happening inside these potatoes on a molecular level. Potatoes are, as you know, very starchy. They're packed with these long chains of glucose molecules called amylose and amylopectin. When we cook them, the heat and the water cause these starch granules to swell up and gelatinize. This makes them easy for our bodies to digest and break down into sugar for energy.

And that's fine. We need energy. But here's the cool part.

**(He walks back to the counter and picks up a container of pre-cooked, chilled potatoes from his fridge.)**

When you take these cooked potatoes and you cool them down... I'm talking a good, long chill in the refrigerator, at least a few hours, preferably overnight... something amazing happens. It's a process called retrogradation.

Basically, as the starches cool, they start to recrystallize. They form new structures that are much more "resistant" to the digestive enzymes in our small intestine. This is what we call resistant starch type 3, or RS3.

**(He holds up the container to the camera.)**

So these potatoes, which are chemically almost identical to the ones boiling on my stove, are now a very different food from a digestive perspective. A significant portion of the starch in here is now going to travel all the way down to your large intestine, where it becomes a feast for your gut microbiome.

**(Scene change: The potatoes are cooked and drained. Adam is now dicing some celery and red onion.)**

Alright, our potatoes are cooked and now comes the most important, and also the easiest, step: we're going to let them cool. Completely. I'm going to spread them out on a tray here to speed things up a bit.

**(He spreads the potatoes on a baking sheet.)**

Now, while that's happening, let's put together the rest of our potato salad. I'm not going to be too prescriptive here. You know how you like your potato salad. For me, it's some finely diced celery for crunch, a little bit of red onion for a bit of a bite.

**(He mixes the celery and onion in a large bowl.)**

For the dressing, I'm keeping it simple. A good dollop of mayonnaise... and yes, you can make your own, but let's be real... some Dijon mustard, a splash of white wine vinegar, and a good pinch of salt and pepper.

**(He whisks the dressing ingredients together.)**

Now, a lot of people will tell you to dress your potatoes while they're still warm, so they absorb more of the flavor. And they're not wrong. But for our purposes today, we're intentionally waiting. We want those starches to retrograde.

**(He gestures to the cooling potatoes.)**

And here's another interesting little tidbit from the science. Some studies have shown that even if you reheat these cooled potatoes, a lot of that resistant starch remains. So, if you're not a fan of cold potato salad, you could gently warm this up before serving and still get many of the benefits.

**(Scene change: The potatoes are now cool. Adam adds them to the bowl with the dressing and other ingredients.)**

So, our potatoes are cool to the touch. And now, we just gently fold everything together. You don't want to mash them up too much.

**(He gently folds the salad.)**

Now, here's the thing. You could eat this right now, and it would be a perfectly delicious potato salad. I've had a little taste. It's good.

**(He takes a small bite.)**

But the real magic happens if you cover this and put it in the fridge until tomorrow. That's when those resistant starch levels are going to be at their peak.

**(He covers the bowl with plastic wrap.)**

So why should we care about this? Well, feeding our gut bacteria with prebiotics like resistant starch is linked to all sorts of good things. It can help improve our insulin sensitivity, it can make us feel fuller for longer, and the byproducts of that fermentation in our gut, things like butyrate, are really important for the health of our colon cells.

Now, it's not a miracle cure for anything. And if you suddenly start eating a ton of resistant starch, you might get a little... gassy. So, you know, ease into it. But it's a simple, evidence-based way to make a classic comfort food just a little bit better for you.

**(Final shot: Adam is at his counter with the finished bowl of potato salad. He takes a satisfying bite.)**

So there you have it. A potato salad that's not just a side dish, but a little science experiment in your own kitchen. You're not just making food, you're transforming it. And all it takes is a little bit of patience.

**(He smiles at the camera.)**

Give it a try. Let me know what you think. And I'll see you next time.

Content:
19:08 Oh boy you pulled that around perfectly there.

As others have observed this video seems particularly personal/emotional, which is completely fine but I do think some points are exaggerated/slanted.

I mostly disagree with the hard assertions that LLMs don't know or think. Clearly there is information encoded in these networks, ChatGPT can perfectly recite the first 1000 digits of pi as well as answer a whole load of trivia questions, which means it clearly contains/'knows' a lot of facts.
As for thinking, as far as I can tell there is no consistent answer to what thinking even is. One definition I found is "a complex mental process involving manipulating internal representations like ideas, images, and symbols to solve problems, make decisions, and understand the world", which sounds an awful lot like "word math". Now that particular definition came from the Google AI search summary so don't put too much weight in that specific one. My point is that the detailed psychology of both LLMs and humans is far from understood and many terms like 'thinking' can be defined in a way that includes LLMs. To say all those definitions are categorically wrong because of that is not very scientific.

I do agree with your use of the terms 'bullshitting' and 'lying', I think that that is much more appropriate than 'hallucinating'. It is really hard to train an LLM in a way that prevents this as you'd have to fact-check every single word it produces. The journalist/politician analogy is extremely apt here.

Content:
There are massive issues with AI, I'm not trying to claim otherwise. But it's a pretty weak argument to say, "It's okay when humans lie because they lie in predictable ways and we can shame them. RFK's MAHA report wouldn't have been any better if a human wrote it - I could have written that report, and through very selective wording and cherry picking what to cite, it would have been even less truthful without making anything up. My dad gets all his news from crap he reads on the internet and his very opinionated, very partisan neighbor. My dad would no doubt be better off if ChatGPT would fact check all of this. I've heard countless stories of people having their very real health problems dismissed by an arrogant doctor - ChatGPT is obviously worse than a great doctor, but is it worse than the average healthcare experience for a lot of people, especially once you factor in accessibility? Probably not. I guess my point is that I agree with Adam about AI, but massively disagree with him about how good people are.

Before someone calls me a tech bro, I think it's sad that a lot of climate change progress is being set back by the massive data centers needed to power LLMs. It's also worrying that so many people pass off the work of LLMs as their own, and no doubt LLMs are trained on dubiously collected material. Author: @AleksandarStefanovic
Content:
I agree and disagree on a couple of points — I agree that they're just statistical algorithms (and everything that ever happens on a computer is an algorithm), but, based on that point, I disagree on personifying the algorithms "they don't think, they have no shame", as that is missing the point that everything that happens on a computer is just moving electrical signals, through conductors, to and from memory storage — unless the solution is to add a shame algorithm to the statistical model.

Also, antagonizing any tool in general is unconstructive. It is useful to know the correct uses, the potential caveats, and the motivation behind the people creating these tools. IMO, it should be better to have a sentiment of "If you're familiar with the domain of your question, and can easily verify the result given by the LLM, go ahead and use it, but beware when inquiring about something completely unfamiliar, as it may produce a false statement that you have no way of checking, and the model will do so with utmost confidence.".

Author: @wingbeltcreations5455
Content:
Edit: All of you have had me realize how poorly I explained my stance on this, so I'm going to put some more context. Looking back on this comment, it's a classic example to not boil down such a nuanced topic into just a few sentences.

My core point is that "AI" as a term can refer to a wide variety of technologies, as there are not widely adopted standards for what the TERM "AI" means, especially for those who are less tech savvy. "AI" can be colloquially used to describe any algorithm or software, from something as simple from the Pac-Man Ghosts to as complex as modern LLMs. For example, 20 year old games refer to computer-controlled characters as "AI" and "CPU", even though that's not what EITHER of those terms LITERALLY refer to. Media like The Terminator is brought up often in these conversations as "Artificial Intelligence", when a near-sentient and fully capable robot is not even CLOSE to our current technologies. But in casual conversation, these terms and examples communicate what they need to, and can skew the definitions and understanding of them when the actual technologies are discussed.

I have explained to my boss that specific startups "don't use an LLM, but they DO have an algorithm that DOES achieve what they say it will according to their patents and documentation, but is NOT "AI" by the modern definition which involves LLMs." I make the comparison between low-level algorithms and an LLM to demonstrate the power of marketing and how that term, ESPECIALLY to those that haven't researched the technology, baseless claims can be made and exploit that lack of knowledge in others.

To be clear, I'm not saying that an LLM is as complex as a Pac-Man ghost, or that innovation can be brushed aside as in the examples below of the "Horse vs. Car" or the "Refrigerator vs. Icebox," but rather that people can slap the label of "Refrigerator" on an icebox, or abuse the term "horsepower" and dress a horse up in a costume to look like a car, and mislead those who didn't check under the hood.

As frustrating as I find this industry, I won't deny that I improperly made my argument, and I do apologize for causing so much confusion in this thread.



From here on is my original comment:

I work for an investment company. The amount of "AI" startups that come through are absurd, and every time I have to re-explain to my entire office what "AI" actually does, and what it can't do.


My favorite line to say is that "AI is, in a practical sense,  just a term to describe an algorithm. The Ghosts from Pac-Man in 1980 had an 'AI'."

Author: @Marc-Davis
Content: This is a better anti-AI argument than most, because it doesn't rely on AI being generally poor in quality, but poor in inherently AI-specific ways. If your only complaint about AI is that it doesn't work very well, the obvious question raised is, "what about when it does work well?" For my money, the worst thing about AI (specifically in creative areas like writing or visual art) is that it threatens to corrupt our understanding of what writing/drawing "well" is. It's an aggregation machine, and if its outputs infiltrate the culture enough, we'll start to understand standard "good" writing as an aggregated, bland, center. It then, through the culture at large, changes our perception of good writing (and therefore, in some senses, good thought) to meet its output, pushing human writing towards its aggregated, bland, center. It's a critique of mass culture accelerated to, potentially, an absurd degree.

Content:
I am generally glad that, after taking money from companies to promote their gAI products, Adam has finally decided to stake his position on his values regarding gAI. It's unfortunate that he had to finally come to this conclusion after seeing the tip of the iceberg when it comes to its proliferation into government.

Here's a few things that I think should make you hate gAI in addition to "the existence of the MAHA report is dystopic":
1. It exploits CSAM and snuff content scraped from the internet and laundered through massive data sets.
2. It exploits global south slave labor to sort, categorize, and manually filter its training data, who often have their atrociously small wages stolen (a subject of ongoing lawsuits), and who are exposed with no support systems to traumatizing material (see: point 1 above)
3. The data centers being built here in the US suck up the drinking water of the communities they're built in, making them lose potable water availability, consume excessive amounts of power, causing outages and brownouts in those communities, need to supplement their power draw with on-site generators that burn fossil fuels and exhaust the byproduct into the communities, and all of which are being done largely in historically marginalized and racialized communities who have little to no power to say whether or not they want their community and environment exploited and polluted in such a way.

They were pro-technology, many of them engineers themselves. They were, however, opposed to their bosses using the fruits of their labor to purchase capital that would be used to obsolete them with no share or compensation. It’s hardly the most egregious, harmful example, but I’ll tell the story that destroyed my faith in this garbage:
I was writing this story featuring a bunch of creatures out of different real world folklores and mythologies and the like. I’d recently seen South Park’s chatGPT episode and thought the idea of treating it like a writing assistant seemed reasonable. So I gave it a list of what I wanted- what parts of the world to draw from, what magical abilities, all that. It spat me out a couple ideas… but when I went to look up the creatures it mentioned, I couldn’t find what it was talking about. So I asked it to cite its sources. It did, with a couple obscure old texts and books. I found them on the Internet Archive anyway, checked the page numbers, and confirmed- the damned thing not only made up its facts, it made up its sources.
Never again.

Author: @danielminor5595
Content:
I’m a fan of AI, and use it often, but this is a very valid concern. 

Rather than admit that a ‘deeper dive’ is needed, AI will just straight up lie to you. When I ask AI a question that I think it’ll likely lie to me about (like anything involving recent news), I’ll often have to prompt the AI multiple times just to confirm a truth e.g. “What controversial thing did the president say two days ago. Are you certain that’s what he said, and that you’re pulling from the correct day? Can you cross reference that against articles? Can you link me to those articles and confirm it?”

I’m certain there’s been plenty of times where I haven’t even thought to do this tho, and interpreted one of its well-spoken lies as a truth.

Author: @Widowmaker104
Content:
If you only trained an AI on your content and took away any underlying built-in prompts it would sound way more similar. Of course it sounds off when its training data is the entire internet or whatever data it uses.
AI content farms do suck and should probably be against TOS on many platforms since it only serves to take up server space and frustrate users.
But, from my experience using AI as an assistant and learning tool it has truly been profoundly helpful, factual and correct. 
I was learning a DAW (digital audio workstation) for the first time and had to figure out what all the thousands of options on the screen where for and just asking ChatGPT for help saved me a ton of time that i would have otherwise had to spent sifting though different youtube "tutorials" that always want to sell you overpriced courses and long forum threads of equally incompetent users debating each other on how to solve a given problem.
It was not just "regurgitating word salads" but actually gave in depth, detailed explanations on how to do specific things within the program and whenever i did as it said it worked.
Yes, AI has problems and weaknesses but soo many people use motivated reasoning to argue it sucks, not because it sucks but because they want it to suck since it scares them in some way.
Maybe those fears are granted but that does not justify being biased against the facts.
